turns.q: something has been nagging me about nvidia. the earnings look spectacular but is the cash actually showing up behind them? I want to know whether the profits are real
turns.answer:
The earnings do look real in the cash flow: NVDA’s 12-month operating cash flow rose from $5.82B to $103B, while free cash flow margin was 30.2%, 14.1%, 44.4%, 46.6%, and 44.8%, so the profits have been turning into cash rather than just accounting profit.
The quality check is not perfect, though: NVDA’s accruals ratio was -5.18%, 1.46%, -3.09%, 2.54%, 7.88%, and 8.39%. That means cash has mostly kept up, but the most recent years show profits growing faster than operating cash flow relative to assets, so the book would read this as strong but not “all-clear” earnings quality.
One thing I cannot yet state from the desk is a direct free-cash-flow amount for every period, because the computed result gave the margin series but not a standalone cash figure for each window. If you want, I can next pull the exact free cash flow series, or I can check working-capital drivers and capex to see what is driving the gap between earnings and cash.

turns.q: for nvidia, are receivables and inventory growing faster than the top line? that's usually what you see before demand rolls over
turns.answer:
Yes: on the latest comparable quarter in the desk’s series, NVDA’s receivables are growing faster than revenue, and inventory is too. Accounts receivable is up 126.8% year over year, while revenue is up 61.4% year over year. Inventory is up 111.0% year over year, also faster than revenue. That is the kind of mix that can precede a demand slowdown, but this desk only shows the working-capital pattern; it does not, by itself, prove rollover.
The stronger warning is receivables: the series shows a sharp step-up into 2026-07-26, and the growth rate is well above top-line growth on the same comparison. Inventory is elevated too, but less extreme than receivables on the latest yoy point. If you want, I can next compare these to gross margin, days sales outstanding, and inventory turns to see whether this is just growth scaling or a genuine demand/collection problem.

turns.q: walk me through the worst drawdown this book has had over the last year — how deep, how fast, and did we get it back
turns.answer:
The worst drawdown over the last year was 12.0%, a 11.96% peak-to-trough decline from 2026-01-07 to 2026-03-27. It took 55 sessions to reach the trough, and the book got back to the prior peak by 2026-05-01 after 24 more sessions.
How fast it fell: the drawdown ran for 55 sessions from peak to trough, then recovered in 24 sessions. The next-largest episode was much smaller, 6.24% at 6.24% from 2026-05-29 to 2026-06-25, with recovery in 13 sessions.
Did we get it back? Yes: the deepest episode is marked recovered true, with recovery_date 2026-05-01. On the fixed-window replay from 2026-01-08 to 2026-03-27, the book returned -11.96% versus SPY at -7.8%, so the book fell more than the market over the same window.
What drove that drop in the fixed-window replay: every holding was negative except XOM, which returned +45.27%; the worst individual movers were MSFT at -26.04%, LLY at -20.61%, AMZN at -17.48%, and GOOGL at -14.74%. The desk also says this replay does not decompose the drawdown's depth itself, so these are the window returns that correspond to the episode, not an additive explanation of the peak-to-trough loss.

Amazon’s capex was $151B and depreciation was $45.64B, so capex ran at 330.9%× depreciation. Both are investing well above their current depreciation run-rate, and Amazon is the more stretched of the two by this measure.
The cash-flow picture points the same way but with different severity: Microsoft still generated positive free cash flow of $72.92B, while Amazon’s free cash flow was $-2.47B, meaning capex exceeded operating cash flow over the period. That is a much clearer sign of infrastructure spend outrunning near-term internally generated cash for Amazon.
What this does not tell us is whether either company is over-investing in an economic sense, because the desk does not hold a filed figure for return on that capex. What it does show is that both are spending above depreciation, and Amazon’s spending is also above operating cash flow on the latest annual window.

turns.q: apple against microsoft — whose gross margin is holding up better, and is that mix or pricing?
turns.answer:
MSFT’s gross margin is holding up better than AAPL’s: MSFT is at 68.3%, while AAPL is at 47.9%. On trend, AAPL’s last four annual gross margins rose from 43.3% to 46.9%, while MSFT’s rose to 68.8% but then dipped from its prior peak, so MSFT is still higher but AAPL’s line has been the steadier riser.
That points more to pricing and mix than to raw cost pressure. AAPL’s gross margin improved from 43.3% to 46.9%, which is consistent with favorable mix or pricing; MSFT stayed near the high end of its own recent range and only softened a touch at the latest point, which also looks like mix/pricing resilience rather than a broad margin-cost collapse. I would not call this a clean cost story from gross margin alone.
If you want, I can separate mix from pricing more cleanly by checking gross margin against revenue growth and segment/product notes in filings; gross margin by itself does not prove which one did the work.

turns.q: if I wanted to take that down without selling the biggest position, what are my options
turns.answer:
You can take concentration down without touching the biggest position, but the trade has to be aimed at the next-most-important names rather than the top one. The book’s largest issuer weight on the current run is JPM at 14.9% = 14.86% of the book as of 2026-09-04; the other big names shown on that same run are LLY at 12.7% = 12.70% and XOM at 4.41% = 4.41%. The sector shape is still dominated by Technology at 35.1% = 35.08%, with Financials at 14.9% = 14.86%, Healthcare at 12.7% = 12.70%, and Energy at 4.41% = 4.41%.
I tested one example trim: selling 25% of JPM on the latest run. That would sell 25.0% = 25% of JPM, or $403K = $403,470, and leave the book at $10.46M = $10,456,222 in market value. JPM would fall to 11.6% = 11.58% of the book in the after-book, while the biggest positions would remain MSFT at 16.7% = 16.73%, AAPL at 15.3% = 15.30%, and LLY at 13.2% = 13.19%.
The important part is what still bites after that trim: the scenario still shows issuer concentration warnings on AAPL, LLY, and MSFT, while sector concentration stays okay. So trimming JPM helps single-name and Financials exposure, but it does not by itself fix the book’s overall concentration problem.
Your practical options, in order, are: trim JPM further; trim LLY, which is the next largest visible holding; trim MSFT or AAPL if the point is to reduce the whole-book concentration rather than just Financials; or pair a trim in the largest sector names with a redeployment into smaller or less-correlated positions, if you want to keep the book invested but less lopsided.
